topic: Should Toronto residential property taxes be held to inflation or below (Bradford), or remain a primary lever for fiscal sustainability with at-or-above-inflation increases plus progressive add-ons (Chow)?
pull_quote: Toronto's residential rate ran at or below inflation for most of 2010 to 2022, then rose 7.0 percent in 2023, 9.5 percent in 2024, and 6.9 percent in 2025 before the 2026 budget settled at 2.2 percent. The ten-year capital plan grew to $63.1 billion in 2026, with an $18 billion state-of-good-repair gap still outstanding.

who_benefits.intro: Each candidate's stance shifts incidence between current owner-occupiers, renters, the non-residential base, and users of city services that depend on the capital plan. The property-tax incidence literature offers competing views (the benefit view, the new view, and assessment-regressivity work) that bracket the same trade-off.

mechanisms.summary: Restraint at or below inflation reduces the year-over-year cash burden on owner-occupiers and pass-through to tenants in the short run. Property tax incidence research is split: from the perspective of a single jurisdiction the local tax is borne mainly by local residents and is roughly proportional to housing consumption (Mieszkowski and Zodrow, 1989), and assessment-based regressivity has been documented at the national level in U.S. data (Avenancio-Leon and Howard, 2022). However, Toronto's own infrastructure backlog means restraint shifts cost into deferred capital, debt service, or service reductions whose incidence falls on transit riders, social housing tenants, and users of city facilities.

At-or-above-inflation residential increases plus progressive add-ons (3 percent Vacant Home Tax, graduated luxury MLTT to 8.6 percent) raise the immediate cash burden on owner-occupiers while drawing additional revenue from non-occupied units and high-value transactions. The new view of property tax incidence holds that the nationwide-average burden falls on capital owners and is progressive, while the above-average local component drives capital out of high-tax jurisdictions and is borne by local residents (Mieszkowski, 1972; Zodrow, 2001). Tassonyi, Bird, and Slack (2015) found GTA municipalities had not exhausted the revenue-raising side of the property tax curve, suggesting room to raise rates without crossing the revenue-hill peak, though they flagged tax-competition effects between Toronto and surrounding municipalities.

positions.summary: In his 2023 mayoral byelection platform Bradford committed to keep property tax increases at or below the rate of inflation. In council, he voted against the 2025 6.9 percent increase, called it a record-breaking tax increase, and on the 2026 budget pressed Mayor Chow on whether she would commit to keeping property taxes at the rate of inflation in a future term, characterizing the 2026 reduction as a pre-election move financed from reserves.

positions.summary: Chow's three budgets delivered a 9.5 percent residential increase in 2024, 6.9 percent in 2025, and 2.2 percent in 2026, with the lower 2026 figure attributed to revenue from progressive levies (3 percent Vacant Home Tax, graduated luxury MLTT) rather than a permanent shift in approach. On the 2024 budget Chow noted that closing the $1.776 billion opening pressure with residential property taxes alone would have required a 42 percent increase.

status_quo.summary: What is actually happening in Toronto now (2026 budget, adopted February 10, 2026): operating budget of $18.9 billion ($16.61 billion tax-supported, $2.25 billion rate-supported); ten-year capital plan of $63.1 billion (2026 to 2035); 2026 residential property tax increase of 0.7 percent base plus 1.5 percent City Building Fund equals 2.2 percent combined; approximate annual impact on the typical home of about $91.53 per year; state-of-good-repair gap of $18 billion over the next decade as of 2025, down from a previously reported $26 billion.

comparables.name: Toronto
comparables.summary: Year-by-year total residential increases (base plus dedicated levies) ranged from 0.0 percent in 2011 to 9.5 percent in 2024. Under restraint years (Ford-era 2011 to 2014 and the early Tory era through 2019), Toronto's state-of-good-repair backlog grew. Under the 2024 to 2025 increases, the city reported $8 billion of progress against the renewal gap and a $63.1 billion ten-year capital plan in 2026.
comparables.outcome: Restraint years coincided with deteriorating municipal infrastructure per IMFG analysis; expansion years (2024 to 2025) produced an $8 billion reduction in the state-of-good-repair gap.

citations.label: Slack and IMFG, Canadian Municipal Fiscal Sustainability, 2024
CBC News, Toronto state-of-good-repair backlog reporting, 2025
Ontario Construction News, Toronto 10-year capital plan, 2026

comparables.caveats: Tax history mixes base rate, Scarborough Subway levy, and City Building Fund levy. Pandemic-era operating pressures (refugee shelter costs, transit ridership shortfall) are partial explanations for 2023 to 2025 increases and complicate clean attribution to mayoral preference.

comparables.name: Calgary
comparables.summary: Calgary council approved a plan in November 2023 to shift one percentage point of total tax share from non-residential to residential properties each year from 2024 through 2026, with a 2024 residential increase of 7.8 percent paired with 3.5 percent non-residential. In November 2025, council cancelled the planned 1 percent shift for 2026 and reduced the overall 2026 increase to 1.64 percent.
comparables.outcome: Residential tax share moved from roughly 52:48 toward 55:45 then partially reversed. The 2026 reduction was achieved through reserve reallocation rather than a permanent revenue source.

citations.label: CTV Calgary, Council shifts tax share from non-residential to residential, 2023
CBC Calgary, Council approves 3.6% increase for 2025, 2024
City of Calgary, 2026 Budget update, 2025
Sprawl Calgary, 2026 reduction analysis, 2025

comparables.caveats: Alberta's provincial education property tax adds a separate top-line increase that compounds municipal decisions. Calgary's non-residential base differs in scale from Toronto's and faces sustained downtown office vacancy.

comparables.name: Vancouver Empty Homes Tax
comparables.summary: Vancouver's Empty Homes Tax has generated $194.3 million for affordable housing since 2017 and the number of declared or deemed-vacant homes fell to 979 in 2024, a 0.49 percent vacancy rate. Caracciolo and Miglino (2024) used a difference-in-differences design across the Vancouver and Burnaby boundary and estimated the tax lowered vacancy by 1.5 percentage points and reduced empty units by approximately 5,355 between 2016 and 2021.
comparables.outcome: $194.3 million for affordable housing since 2017; vacancy reduced by 1.5 percentage points (about 5,355 units); no measured effect on average rent.

citations.label: City of Vancouver, Empty Homes Tax annual report, 2025
Caracciolo and Miglino, Vancouver Empty Homes Tax difference-in-differences evaluation, 2024

comparables.caveats: Vancouver and Toronto differ in housing market structure. Toronto's revamped 3 percent Vacant Home Tax projected approximately $105 million in 2024 revenue but has had administrative issues including 2023 declaration program errors that prompted a 2024 program redesign.

comparables.name: Property tax incidence literature
comparables.summary: The benefit view treats property tax as a payment for local services and so as roughly non-distortionary; the new view pioneered by Mieszkowski (1972) treats nationwide-average property tax as a tax on capital owners (progressive) and the above-average local component as borne by local residents through capital outflows. Recent U.S. work documents systematic regressivity in assessment-based incidence at the parcel level. Tassonyi, Bird, and Slack (2015) found GTA municipalities had not reached the revenue-maximizing point on the property tax curve.
comparables.outcome: Theoretical bracketing of incidence: capital-tax incidence is progressive nationally; local incidence on capital outflows is regressive at the jurisdiction margin; assessment-based regressivity is documented at the parcel level. GTA municipalities have available revenue room.

citations.label: Mieszkowski and Zodrow, Taxation and the Tiebout Model, Journal of Economic Literature, 1989
Zodrow, The Property Tax as a Capital Tax, National Tax Journal, 2001
Avenancio-Leon and Howard, The Assessment Gap, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2022
Tassonyi, Bird, and Slack, Can GTA Municipalities Raise Property Taxes? IMFG, 2015

comparables.caveats: The U.S. assessment-regressivity literature uses parcel-level sales-ratio data not directly transferable to MPAC's mass-appraisal regime in Ontario. Theoretical incidence views differ in assumed capital mobility and time horizon and are not directly comparable to a single-year council decision.

projections.intro: Three plural framings the literature does support. Literature does not support a confident singular projection on this question.

items.scenario_label: Sustained restraint (Bradford-style at or below inflation)
items.range_or_value: Continuing growth in the state-of-good-repair backlog absent a substitute revenue source

items.notes: Consistent with the deferred-capital pattern observed in Toronto from roughly 2011 through 2022.

items.range_or_value: Operating-budget stabilization paired with documented annual cost increase relative to a freeze counterfactual

items.notes: Available revenue room exists in the GTA, but tax-competition effects on the non-residential base are documented.

items.notes: These are smaller than the operating-budget gap absorbed by the 2024 9.5 percent increase, so the literature does not support a claim that progressive levies alone substitute for residential rate decisions over a four-year term.

time_horizon: Property tax rate decisions affect household cash flow in year one and accumulate compoundingly across a four-year term. State-of-good-repair effects of restraint or expansion materialize across roughly five to fifteen years as deferred renewal feeds into asset failures and service disruptions. Capital tax incidence effects under the new view are long-run general-equilibrium effects measured across decades.
